reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Hypersomnia denotes excessive daytime sleepiness or an excessive need for sleep that is not explained by insufficient sleep opportunity, and it should be distinguished from fatigue and low motivation
The most common cause overall is chronic insufficient sleep, and this behavioural cause must be excluded before pursuing primary hypersomnia disorders
Secondary hypersomnia from obstructive sleep apnoea, medication or substance effects, depression, and other medical conditions is far more common than the central disorders of hypersomnolence
Narcolepsy, especially type 1 with cataplexy, is the prototypical central hypersomnia and is linked to loss of hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) signalling
Idiopathic hypersomnia produces prolonged, non-refreshing sleep with severe sleep inertia and is a diagnosis of exclusion
The Epworth Sleepiness Scale quantifies subjective sleepiness, while objective assessment relies on polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Documenting short sleep latency and early transitions into REM sleep on testing supports a diagnosis of narcolepsy
Management combines good sleep hygiene, treatment of any underlying cause, scheduled naps, and, on principle, wake-promoting pharmacotherapy where required
reference.pathophysiology: Normal daytime alertness depends on adequate prior sleep and on wake-promoting neuronal systems, prominently the hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) network. In narcolepsy type 1, selective loss of orexin-producing neurons, thought to be autoimmune and associated with specific HLA types, destabilises the boundaries between wake, non-REM, and REM sleep, producing sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations as REM phenomena intrude into wakefulness. Idiopathic hypersomnia has a less well-defined mechanism, possibly involving enhanced GABAergic sedation or altered sleep homeostasis. Secondary hypersomnias arise when sleep is fragmented (as in sleep apnoea or periodic limb movements), curtailed (insufficient sleep), or suppressed in quality by drugs, depression, or systemic illness, reducing restorative sleep and driving daytime sleepiness.
additionalDifferentials: Depression and other psychiatric or medical illness
additionalInvestigations: Detailed sleep history and sleep diary, sometimes with actigraphy, to exclude insufficient sleep
Epworth Sleepiness Scale to quantify subjective daytime sleepiness
Overnight polysomnography to exclude sleep apnoea and other fragmenting disorders
Multiple sleep latency test to measure objective sleepiness and detect early REM onsets
Selected testing such as CSF orexin or HLA typing when narcolepsy is suspected
redFlags: Cataplexy, indicating narcolepsy type 1 and warranting confirmatory evaluation
Sudden severe sleepiness following a central nervous system insult or with new neurological signs
Sleepiness causing motor vehicle or occupational accidents, a safety priority
Hypersomnia masking underlying depression with suicide risk
reference.prognosis: Secondary hypersomnia often improves substantially when the underlying cause is treated; narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia are typically lifelong but manageable, with most patients achieving meaningful symptom control through combined behavioural and pharmacological measures.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude chronic insufficient sleep before diagnosing a primary hypersomnia
Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as a treatable cause of daytime sleepiness
Missing cataplexy in the history and thereby delaying a narcolepsy diagnosis
Neglecting the road-safety and occupational implications of severe daytime sleepiness
management: Treat the underlying cause of secondary hypersomnia, using CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea, reviewing sedating medication and addressing depression
Ensure adequate sleep opportunity and sleep hygiene, with scheduled short naps in central disorders
Wake-promoting agents such as modafinil or armodafinil, or amphetamine-type stimulants, for narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia
Treat cataplexy with sodium oxybate, pitolisant or noradrenergic-serotonergic antidepressants in narcolepsy type 1
Safety counselling on driving and occupational hazards while sleepiness remains uncontrolled
Monitor treatment response with symptom scales and specialist sleep-medicine follow-up
